title: </> htmx ~ Code is Cheap(er)
summary: Concedes code has become much cheaper, but argues understanding has become more expensive and complexity is the main danger, so engineers should constrain and subtract from LLM output.

assertions.quote: While I appreciate the sentiment, I don’t completely agree with that: certainly coding was at least part of the problem.

verdicts.note: Studies of developer time show coding is a minority of work; DORA and Faros 2025 found individual coding gains often don't translate into delivery throughput.

assertions.quote: the LLM can produce code far faster than you, or anyone else, can understand it.

verdicts.note: DORA and field reports show review and verification load growing with AI output, consistent with instability and persistent-debt findings.

assertions.quote: Compilers are deterministic; LLMs are, by design, not

verdicts.note: A historical framing; the analogy is debated because LLM output is non-deterministic, unlike compilers.

assertions.quote: developers still need to understand the underlying code even if it is generated by an LLM.

verdicts.note: Ignoring code entirely leads to drift and debt in real codebases; but spec-driven approaches with code review do work.

assertions.quote: This is why I recommend incremental use of LLMs rather than allowing them to generate massive changelists

verdicts.note: Small batches with fast feedback are a strong DORA predictor of delivery performance; DORA 2024 linked AI to larger batches and lower stability.

assertions.quote: There are times when this can be appropriate, such as in a mechanical refactor

verdicts.note: Refactoring is a relative strength, but studies of LLM refactorings still find behavior-changing errors, so tests or review remain needed.

assertions.quote: LLMs are incapable of fear of complexity, and are prolific coders.

verdicts.note: GitClear and DORA 2025 data show more churn and duplication and lower delivery stability as AI adoption rises; more code means more to maintain.
